newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Waves carry off Britannia as empire ends.
newsitem.headline: Waves carry off Britannia as empire ends.

text.p: Britain departed Hong Kong as it had come 156 years ago, by sea.

The royal yacht Britannia steamed out of Victoria harbour and into history early on Tuesday with Prince Charles and outgoing colonial governor Chris Patten on board, less than an hour after Britain handed the territory back to China.
A Royal Marine band in white tunics and pith helmets played martial tunes from the ship's upper deck as Charles and Patten gazed back at the city, once of the brightest gems in the imperial crown.
Escorted by the frigate HMS Chatham, her decks full of sailors at attention, Britannia received salutes from tugboats which sounded their horns and sprayed jets of water into the air.
Her running lights twinkling in the darkness, the 412-foot royal yacht added a majestic, graceful note to the pomp and pageantry which had marked Britain's last day as Hong Kong's colonial master.

"My God, no matter what you think of the British and of colonialism, how can you not be moved by the sight of that ship?" wondered Robert Trenton, a 42-year American businessman as Britannia pulled away from the pier.

"There are a few times in life when you feel like you're a part of history. The past 24 hours have been one of those times for me. Britain left a magnificent city behind. It's up to the Chinese now to make Hong Kong even better."

Chinese troops had already taken up positions in the Prince of Wales barracks less than 100 metres (yards) from Britannia when she set sail 45 minutes after midnight to applause and cheers from thousands of wellwishers crowding the pier.
In a day filled with emotion-draining ceremony, perhaps the most touching moment had been Chris Patten's departure from Government House after five years as governor.

Under a light rain, head bare and without umbrella, the 53-year old former Conservative Party politician walked among his mostly Chinese staff, many resplendent in starched white military uniforms, shaking hands, dabbing eyes and murmuring goodbye.
Patten was to bite his lip often to control his emotions on a day of lowering flags, nostalgic tunes and soulful bugle calls. More than once, a daughter near his side would shed a tear or two.
The scenes were from a vanished world -- the last sigh of Britain's 19th century imperial might finally giving way to China and the 21st century, which many believe will be hers.
Many British residents and tourists in the festive streets of Hong Kong shed a tear on Monday.
But for most Chinese there was a quiet sense of pride that Hong Kong, for better or worse, was finally back in the fold.
"I look at (Britannia) leaving and I know nothing will ever be the same in Hong Kong again," said a Hong Kong Chinese policeman on the waterfront, who asked not to be identified.
"The future? There are many questions about Hong Kong's future. But Hong Kong will be Chinese, there's no doubt about that."
